sentences.text: Barbosania was an extinct pterosaur from the Aptian to Albian stages of the Romualdo Formation in northeastern Brazil. Its skull measured 392 millimeters in length and featured an elongated shape with a slight upward curve in the snout. Unlike some related pterosaurs, Barbosania lacks a rostral and dentary median sagittal crest on its skull.

Researchers estimate the total body length at 209.5 millimeters, though this figure is notably shorter than the skull length. The skeleton includes thirteen dorsal vertebrae, a unique trait distinguishing it from the normal twelve found in related species.
The first four pairs of teeth in Barbosania are extremely long, forming a rosette adapted for catching slippery prey like fish or squids.
It possesses thirteen dorsal vertebrae, a count that differs from the standard twelve seen in other pterosaurs.

The genus Barbosania was named and described by Ross A. Elgin and Eberhard Frey in 2011. The generic name honors Professor Miguel Barbosa of the Museu de História Natural de Sintra, whose collection holds the type specimen.

The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — consists of an almost complete, partially articulated, and uncompressed skeleton including the skull. This specimen was prepared at the Staatliches Museum für Naturkunde Karlsruhe in Germany.

Barbosania was originally assigned to the superfamily Ornithocheiroidea and the family Ornithocheiridae. In 2019, Pêgas et al. reclassified Barbosania into the clade Targaryendraconia and the family Targaryendraconidae.
Fossil evidence places Barbosania in existence between 119.57 and 113.2 million years ago.
Researchers suggest that several specimens previously assigned to Brasileodactylus might actually belong to Barbosania.
